newsitem.title: USA: Fla. court ruling impact on tobacco stocks small.
newsitem.headline: Fla. court ruling impact on tobacco stocks small.

text.p: Tobacco stocks fell slightly Thursday after a decision by the Florida Supreme Court that refused to overturn the class action status of another smoking-related lawsuit against the industry.
But losses were pared almost as quickly as they were registered and analysts said the price impact would be limited because the decision was already assumed by Wall Street.
"I don't think the stocks are going to get whacked because it was really anticipated that this would happen," said Ronald Morrow, tobacco stocks analyst at Rodman & Renshaw.

Philip Morris Cos Inc shares were off 1/2 at 91-7/8 after falling as low as 90-7/8. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, parent of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, was off 3/8 at 26-1/2, up from 26-1/8. Other tobacco stocks were also modestly lower.

Smith Barney tobacco analyst Martin Feldman said despite the ruling, the largest burden on the plaintiffs was devising a way to make such a large class action -- which could include upwards of two million people -- manageable for trial.
The overwhelming expense of the notification process -- advertising for all plaintiffs who may be appropriate for the case -- is part of the problem.
"It's now up to the attorney, Stanley Rosenblatt, to come up with specific claims, a program for dealing with those claims, and a method for informing all potential plaintiffs," Feldman said.
"All the court has said was that the certification can go ahead. What the court is also saying is, now bring us a plan that works," he said.

Another class-action suit, named Broin and representing about 60,000 flight attendants who are suing the tobacco industry for the effects of second-hand smoke, was upheld as a class but has so far languished because it is so unwieldy.

A potential blockbuster class-action suit against tobacco companies -- the Castano case, which would have attempted to sue the industry on behalf of every U.S. smoker claiming addiction -- had its class status overturned in Lousiana in May.
Chief among the reasons for its demise was the court's belief that it was too huge. Feldman said Rosenblatt's failure to move forward on Broin does not bode well for Engle suit.

Rosenblatt "told the court he was unable to afford the funding to notify the potential plaintiffs in the Broin action, so it would seem to me there's a possibility that this case (Engle), if it doesn't go away, might not move forward because of lack of funding and the problems of bringing a workable class action," Feldman said. "And the Broin case is a much smaller case."

The Engle suit "remains out there as a potentially large threat (but) nothing like Castano. (Philip Morris stock) will get over it. I think the market is not particularly concerned by this, and it hasn't taken it by surprise," Feldman said.
